events.title: Council at Jerusalem
events.summary: Apostles and elders decided that Gentile believers need not be circumcised. It is the New Testament's model for church councils, though it isn't counted among the ecumenical councils.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 1, “The Synod of Jerusalem, and the Compromise between Jewish and Gentile Christianity”

events.title: Fire of Rome and Nero's persecution
events.summary: Nero blamed Christians for the fire of Rome, the first known persecution by the Roman state. Early tradition places the deaths of Peter and Paul in this period.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 1, “The Roman Conflagration and the Neronian Persecution”
events.quote: The first of these imperial persecutions with which the Martyrdom of Peter and Paul is connected by ecclesiastical tradition, took place in the tenth year of Nero’s reign, a.d. 64, and by the instigation of that very emperor to whom Paul, as a Roman citizen, had appealed from the Jewish tribunal.

events.title: Destruction of Jerusalem
events.summary: Roman forces destroyed the city and the Temple, which ended Temple sacrifice and sped the separation of church and synagogue.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 1, “The Jewish War and the Destruction of Jerusalem. A.D. 70”
events.quote: In April, a.d. 70, immediately after the Passover, when Jerusalem was filled with strangers, the siege began.

events.title: The Gnostic challenge
events.summary: Gnostic teachers offered secret knowledge and a lower creator god. Answering them shaped early appeals to apostolic succession, the rule of faith and the canon.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 2, “Meaning, Origin and Character of Gnosticism”
events.quote: More important and more widely spread in the second period was the paganizing heresy, known by the name of Gnosticism.

events.title: Marcion's break with the Roman church
events.summary: Marcion rejected the Old Testament and kept a shortened New Testament of Luke and Paul. His movement was condemned, and scholars debate how far it pushed the church to define its own canon.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 2, “Marcion and his School”

events.title: Montanism
events.summary: The New Prophecy of Montanus in Phrygia claimed new revelation and stricter discipline. It was rejected by church synods, though Tertullian joined it.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 2, “External History of Montanism”
events.quote: All the ascetic, rigoristic, and chiliastic elements of the ancient church combined in Montanism.

events.title: Muratorian list of New Testament books
events.summary: An early list of accepted Christian writings, usually dated to the late second century, though some scholars date it later.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 2, “The Holy Scriptures and the Canon”

events.title: The rule of faith in Irenaeus and Tertullian
events.summary: Writers summarized apostolic teaching in a short rule of faith, an early form of the later creeds.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 2, “The Rule of Faith and the Apostles' Creed”

events.title: Tertullian's Trinitarian language
events.summary: Against Praxeas, Tertullian used the Latin trinitas and spoke of one substance in three persons, wording that shaped later Western theology.
events.source: Easton's Bible Dictionary, “Trinity”
events.quote: from the Lat. trinitas, first used by Tertullian (A.D. 220)

events.title: Decian persecution and the lapsed
events.summary: The first empire-wide persecution required public sacrifice. Whether to restore those who gave in divided the church.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 2, “Persecutions under Decius, and Valerian. a.d. 249-260. Martyrdom of Cyprian”
events.quote: Decius Trajan (249–251), an earnest and energetic emperor, in whom the old Roman spirit once more awoke, resolved to root out the church as an atheistic and seditious sect, and in the year 250 published an edict to all the governors of the provinces, enjoining return to the pagan state religion under the heaviest penalties.

events.title: Novatian schism
events.summary: Novatian formed a rival church at Rome that refused to restore those who lapsed under persecution.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 2, “Church Schisms”
events.quote: If bishop of Rome, he was the first schismatic pope, and forerunner of Novatianus, who was ordained anti pope in 251.83 But the Roman Church must have forgotten or forgiven his schism, for she numbers him among her saints and martyrs, and celebrates his memory on the twenty-second of August.

events.title: Diocletian's persecution
events.summary: The last and severest Roman persecution ordered churches destroyed and Scriptures surrendered.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 2, “The Diocletian Persecution, a.d. 303-311”
events.quote: In 303 Diocletian issued in rapid succession three edicts, each more severe than its predecessor.

events.title: Donatist schism
events.summary: North African Christians split over clergy who had surrendered Scriptures under persecution. Augustine's answer shaped Western teaching on the church and sacraments.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “The Donatist Schism. External History”
events.quote: The beginnings of the Donatist schism appear in the Dioclesian persecution, which revived that controversy concerning church discipline and martyrdom.

events.title: Constantine and the Edict of Milan
events.summary: Christianity became a tolerated religion in the Roman Empire, and the church's relation to the state began to change.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 2, “The Edicts of Toleration. a.d. 311-313”
events.quote: A few months afterwards Constantine met at Milan with his co-regent and brother-in-law, Licinius, and issued a new edict of toleration (313), to which Maximin also, shortly before his suicide (313), was compelled to give his consent at Nicomedia.6 The second edict went beyond the first of 311; it was a decisive step from hostile neutrality to friendly neutrality and protection, and prepared the way for the legal reco …

events.title: Arian controversy begins
events.summary: Arius of Alexandria taught that the Son was created and had a beginning, which set off the central Trinitarian debate of the fourth century.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “The Arian Controversy down to the Council of Nicaea, 318-325”
events.quote: The eternal generation of the Son from the will of the Father was, with Origen, the communication of a divine but secondary substance, and this idea, in the hands of the less devout and profound Arius, who with his more rigid logic could admit no intermediate being between God and the creature, deteriorated to the notion of the primal creature.

events.title: First Council of Nicaea
events.summary: The first council counted as ecumenical. It rejected Arianism and confessed the Son as homoousios, of one substance with the Father.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “The Council of Nicaea, 325”
events.quote: Hither, in the year 325, the twentieth of his reign (therefore the festive vicennalia), the emperor summoned the bishops of the empire by a letter of invitation, putting at their service the public conveyances, and liberally defraying from the public treasury the expenses of their residence in Nicaea and of their return.

events.title: Athanasius's list of the 27 New Testament books
events.summary: His Easter letter of 367 is the earliest known list naming exactly the 27 books of today's New Testament.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 2, “The Holy Scriptures and the Canon”

events.title: Christianity made the imperial religion
events.summary: Theodosius I ordered his subjects to hold the Nicene faith, and Christianity became the religion of the empire.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “From Jovian to Theodosius. a.d. 363-392”

events.title: First Council of Constantinople
events.summary: Reaffirmed Nicaea and affirmed the Holy Spirit's deity. The creed recited today as the Nicene Creed is linked with this council.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “The Final Victory of Orthodoxy, and the Council of Constantinople, 381”

events.title: Jerome's Latin Bible
events.summary: Jerome's translation, later called the Vulgate, became the Bible of the medieval West. He preferred the Hebrew text for the Old Testament.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “The Works of Jerome”
events.quote: The Vulgate takes the first place among the Bible-versions of the ancient church.

events.title: Sack of Rome and Augustine's City of God
events.summary: The Goths sacked Rome in 410. Augustine answered pagan blame for it with The City of God, a lasting Christian account of history.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “Augustine's City of God. Salvianus”
events.quote: Augustine himself answered the charge in his immortal work “On the city of God,” that is, the church of Christ, in twenty-two books, upon which he labored twelve years, from 413 to 426, amidst the storms of the great migration and towards the close of his life.

events.title: Pelagian controversy
events.summary: Augustine and Pelagius disputed sin, free will and grace. Pelagius's teaching was condemned, and Augustine's teaching on grace shaped Western theology.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “External History of the Pelagian Controversy, A.D. 411-431”
events.quote: In the year 411, the two friends, thus united in sentiment, left Rome, to escape the dreaded Gothic King Alaric, and went to Africa.

events.title: Council of Ephesus
events.summary: Condemned Nestorius and affirmed Mary as Theotokos, God-bearer. The Church of the East doesn't accept this council.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “The Ecumenical Council of Ephesus, a.d. 431. The Compromise”
events.quote: Theodosius II., in connection with his Western colleague, Valentinian III., summoned a universal council on Pentecost, a.d. 431, at Ephesus, where the worship of the Virgin mother of God had taken the place of the worship of the light and life dispensing virgin Diana.

events.title: The Robber Council of Ephesus
events.summary: A disputed synod backed Eutyches and was later set aside at Chalcedon. Leo the Great gave it the name "Robber Synod."
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “The Eutychian Controversy. The Council of Robbers, a.d. 449”
events.quote: Leo, in 449, confirmed the decision of the council in several epistles, especially in a letter to Flavian, which forms an epoch in the history, of Christology, and in which he gave a masterly, profound, and clear analysis of the orthodox doctrine of two natures in one person.

events.title: Council of Chalcedon
events.summary: Defined Christ as one person in two natures, without confusion or division. Oriental Orthodox churches don't accept it.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “The Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, A.D. 451”
events.quote: To restore the peace of the empire, the new monarch, in May, 451, in his own name and that of his Western colleague, convoked a general council; not, however, to meet in Italy, but at Nicaea, partly that he might the better control it partly that he might add to its authority by the memories of the first ecumenical council.

events.title: Churches divide over Chalcedon
events.summary: The Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and related churches separated from those accepting Chalcedon. They reject the label Monophysite and prefer miaphysite.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “The Monophysite Controversies”

events.title: Council of Orange
events.summary: A regional council in Gaul rejected semi-Pelagianism and affirmed the need of grace from the beginning of faith.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “Victory of Semi-Augustinianism. Council of Orange, A.D. 529”
events.quote: At the synod of Orange (Arausio) in the year 529, at which Caesarius of Arles was leader, the Semi-Pelagian system, yet without mention of its adherents, was condemned in twenty-five chapters or canons, and the Augustinian doctrine of sin and grace was approved, without the doctrine of absolute or particularistic predestination.

events.title: The Rule of Benedict
events.summary: Benedict of Nursia's rule for Monte Cassino became the pattern of Western monastic life.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “Benedict of Nursia”

events.title: Second Council of Constantinople
events.summary: Condemned the Three Chapters in an attempt to reconcile those who rejected Chalcedon. It didn't heal the division.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 3, “The Three, Chapters, and the Fifth Ecumenical Council, A.D. 553”
events.quote: To put an end to this controversy, Justinian, without the concurrence of the pope, convoked at Constantinople, a.d. 553, the Fifth Ecumenical Council, which consisted of a hundred and sixty-four bishops, and held eight sessions, from the 5th of May to the 2d of June, under the presidency of the patriarch Eutychius of Constantinople.

events.title: Filioque at the Council of Toledo
events.summary: The Spanish church's creed at Toledo included "and the Son," a Western addition that became a main dispute with the East.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 4, “The Arguments for and against the Filioque”

events.title: Papacy of Gregory the Great
events.summary: Gregory strengthened the Roman see, sent a mission to England and shaped medieval pastoral practice.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 4, “The Mission of Gregory and Augustin. Conversion of Kent, a.d. 595-604”
events.quote: Pope Gregory I., when abbot of a Benedictine convent, saw in the slave-market of Rome three Anglo-Saxon boys offered for sale.

events.title: Rise of Islam
events.summary: Arab conquests took the Christian lands of Syria, Palestine, Egypt and North Africa, and reshaped the church's geography.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 4, “Mediaeval Christianity”

events.title: Third Council of Constantinople
events.summary: Rejected Monotheletism and confessed two wills in Christ, following Maximus the Confessor's teaching.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 4, “The Sixth Oecumenical Council. a.d. 680”
events.quote: It convened in the imperial palace at Constantinople, and held eighteen sessions from Nov. 7, 680, to Sept. 16, 681. it is called the Sixth Oecumenical, and also the First Trullan Synod, from the name of the hall or chapel in the palace.

events.title: The iconoclastic controversy begins
events.summary: Byzantine emperors moved against religious images, which divided the Eastern church for more than a century.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 4, “The Iconoclastic War, and the Synod of 754”
events.quote: The history of the image-controversy embraces three periods: 1) The war upon images and the abolition of image-worship by the Council of Constantinople, a.d. 726–754. 2) The reaction in favor of image-worship, and its solemn sanction by the second Council of Nicaea, a.d. 754–787. 3) The renewed conflict of the two parties and the final triumph of image-worship, a.d. 842.

events.title: Second Council of Nicaea
events.summary: Restored the veneration of images and distinguished it from worship. Protestants generally don't accept this council.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 4, “The Restoration of Image-Worship by the Seventh Oecumenical Council, 787”

events.title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
events.summary: The pope crowned Charlemagne in Rome, which tied the Western church to a new empire and widened the distance from Constantinople.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 4, “Mediaeval Christianity”

events.title: Final restoration of images in the East
events.summary: Images were restored for good in the East, an event the Orthodox still mark as the Triumph of Orthodoxy.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 4, “Iconoclastic Reaction, and Final Triumph of Image-Worship, a.d. 842”

events.title: Gottschalk and the predestination dispute
events.summary: The monk Gottschalk taught double predestination and was condemned, in a controversy later cited in Reformation debates.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 4, “The Predestinarian Controversy”

events.title: Photian schism
events.summary: Pope Nicholas and Patriarch Photius excommunicated each other in a dispute over authority and the Filioque.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 4, “The Patriarch and the Pope. Photius and Nicolas”
events.quote: The first serious outbreak of this conflict took place after the middle of the ninth century, when Photius and Nicolas, two of the ablest representatives of the rival churches, came into collision.

events.title: The monastery of Cluny
events.summary: Cluny's independence from lay control became the base of a broad monastic reform.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 4, “The Convent of Cluny”
events.quote: It was founded by the pious Duke William of Aquitania in 910, to the honor of St.

events.title: East-West Schism
events.summary: Rome's legates and Patriarch Cerularius excommunicated each other at Constantinople. Historians see this as one stage in a longer separation.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 4, “Progress and Completion of the Schism. Cerularius”
events.quote: Finally, on the 16th of July, 1054, they excommunicated the patriarch and all those who should persistently censure the faith of the church of Rome or its mode of offering the holy sacrifice.

events.title: Investiture conflict and Canossa
events.summary: Emperor Henry IV sought absolution from Gregory VII at Canossa, in the struggle over who appointed bishops.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 5, “Canossa. 1077”
events.quote: The winter of 1076–1077 was one of the coldest and longest within the memory of men—the Rhine being frozen to a solid mass from November till April—and one of the most memorable in history—being marked by an event of typical significance.

events.title: First Crusade
events.summary: Urban II's call at Clermont led to the capture of Jerusalem, with lasting effects on relations with Muslims, Jews and Eastern Christians.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 5, “The Call to the Crusades”
events.quote: The call which resulted in the first expedition for the recovery of Jerusalem was made by Pope Urban II. at the Council of Clermont, 1095.

events.title: Anselm's Cur Deus Homo
events.summary: Anselm explained the atonement as satisfaction for the honor owed to God, a turning point in Western thinking on the cross.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 5, “Anselm of Canterbury”

events.title: Concordat of Worms
events.summary: A compromise over the investiture of bishops between Pope Callistus II and Emperor Henry V.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 5, “The Concordat of Worms. 1122”

events.title: The Waldensian movement
events.summary: Peter Waldo's followers preached poverty and the Scriptures in the common tongue, and were condemned. The Waldensian church survives today.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 5, “The Waldenses”
events.quote: Distinct from the Cathari and other sects in origin and doctrine, but sharing with them the condemnation of the established Church, were the Waldenses.

events.title: Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
events.summary: Crusaders captured and sacked the Eastern capital, which hardened the division between East and West.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 5, “The Fourth Crusade and the Capture of Constantinople. 1200-1204”

events.title: Franciscans and Dominicans
events.summary: New mendicant orders brought preaching and poverty to the growing towns of Europe.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 5, “St. Francis d'Assisi”
events.quote: High up in the list of hagiography stands the name of Francis of Assisi, the founder of the order of the Franciscans.

events.title: Fourth Lateran Council
events.summary: Under Innocent III it used the word transubstantiation in a conciliar decree and required yearly confession. Catholics count it as ecumenical.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 5, “The Fourth Lateran Council, 1215”
events.quote: The council was held in the Lateran and had three sittings, Nov. 11, 20, 30, 1215.

events.title: Papal Inquisition organized
events.summary: Church courts were organized to prosecute heresy, with force supplied by civil rulers.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 5, “The Inquisition. Its Origin and Purpose”
events.quote: The measures for the repression and extermination of heresy culminated in the organized system, known as the Inquisition.

events.title: Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica
events.summary: Aquinas brought Aristotle's philosophy into a large synthesis of Christian theology, the height of scholasticism.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 5, “Thomas Aquinas”

events.title: Unam Sanctam
events.summary: Boniface VIII's bull made one of the strongest medieval claims for papal authority.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 6, “Boniface VIII. and Philip the Fair of France”
events.quote: The second is one of the most notable of all papal documents, the bull Unam sanctam, the name given to it from its first words, "We are forced to believe in one holy Catholic Church." It marks an epoch in the history of the declarations of the papacy, not because it contained anything novel, but because it set forth with unchanged clearness the stiffest claims of the papacy to temporal and spiritual power.

events.title: The papacy at Avignon
events.summary: The popes lived at Avignon in France for nearly seventy years, which damaged their standing across Europe.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 6, “The Transfer of the Papacy to Avignon”
events.quote: After holding his court at Bordeaux, Poictiers, and Toulouse, he chose, in 1309, Avignon as his residence.

events.title: Western Schism
events.summary: Rival popes, at one point three, divided Western Europe until the Council of Constance ended the split.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 6, “The Schism Begun. 1378”
events.quote: On April 7, 1378, ten days after Gregory’s death, the conclave met in the Vatican, and the next day elected the Neapolitan, Bartholomew Prignano, archbishop of Bari.

events.title: Wyclif and the English Bible
events.summary: John Wyclif challenged papal claims and transubstantiation, and inspired an English translation of the Bible.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 6, “Wyclif and the Scriptures”
events.quote: Wyclif’s chief service for his people, next to the legacy of his own personality, was his assertion of the supreme authority of the Bible for clergy and laymen alike and his gift to them of the Bible in their own tongue.

events.title: Council of Constance and the burning of Hus
events.summary: The council ended the Western Schism, asserted its own authority and condemned John Hus, who was burned in 1415.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 6, “The Council of Constance. 1414-1418”

events.title: Council of Ferrara-Florence
events.summary: Greek and Latin delegates signed a union of the churches, including the Filioque. Most in the East rejected it.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 6, “The Council of Ferrara-Florence. 1438-1445”
events.quote: After sixteen sessions held at Ferrara, Eugenius transferred the council, February, 1439, to Florence.

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.summary: The Ottoman capture ended the Byzantine Empire and placed the Eastern patriarchate under Ottoman rule.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 6, “History of the Christian Church, Volume VI”
events.quote: In 1453, Constantinople easily passed into the hands of the Turk, and the Christian empire of the East fell apart.

events.title: Erasmus's Greek New Testament
events.summary: The first published Greek New Testament, the root of the Textus Receptus behind the KJV and other Reformation Bibles.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 7, “Erasmus”

events.title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
events.summary: Luther's challenge to the sale of indulgences is usually taken as the start of the Protestant Reformation.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 7, “The Ninety-five Theses. Oct. 31, 1517”

events.title: Diet of Worms
events.summary: Luther refused to recant before Charles V and was outlawed, after the pope had excommunicated him.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 7, “The Diet of Worms. 1521”
events.quote: But its greatest fame the city acquired by Luther’s heroic stand on the word of God and the rights of conscience, which made the Diet of 1521 one of the most important in the history of German Diets.

events.title: Reformation in Zurich
events.summary: Zwingli's Sixty-seven Articles led to Zurich's break with Rome and the beginning of the Reformed tradition.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 8, “Modern Christianity. The Swiss Reformation.”

events.title: Anabaptists begin in Zurich
events.summary: Conrad Grebel and others began baptizing believers. Their movement was persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 8, “Modern Christianity. The Swiss Reformation.”
events.quote: At a private religious meeting, Blaurock asked Grebel to give him the true Christian baptism on confession of his faith, fell on his knees and was baptized.

events.title: Schleitheim Confession
events.summary: The first known Anabaptist confession, covering believers' baptism, separation from the world, and the refusal of arms and oaths.
events.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Schleitheim Confession”
events.quote: the first known Anabaptist confession

events.title: Marburg Colloquy
events.summary: Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen articles but not on Christ's presence in the Supper, which left the two Protestant streams apart.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 7, “The Marburg Conference, a.d. 1529. (With Facsimile of Signatures.”

events.title: Augsburg Confession
events.summary: Melanchthon's statement of Lutheran faith, presented to Charles V, and still the chief Lutheran confession.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 7, “The Augsburg Confession”

events.title: English church breaks with Rome
events.summary: Parliament's Act of Supremacy made Henry VIII head of the Church of England.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “V. the Anglican Articles of Religion.”

events.title: Calvin's Institutes
events.summary: Calvin's first edition appeared at Basel. Expanded through 1559, it became the classic statement of Reformed theology.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 8, “Calvin's Institutes of the Christian Religion”

events.title: Calvin returns to Geneva
events.summary: Calvin's church order in Geneva became a model for Reformed churches across Europe.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 8, “Calvin's Return to Geneva. 1541”

events.title: Council of Trent
events.summary: The Catholic answer to the Reformation defined Scripture and tradition, justification and the seven sacraments, and reformed church discipline.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Canons and Decrees of the Council of Trent, A.D. 1563.”

events.title: Consensus of Zurich
events.summary: Calvin and Bullinger agreed on the Lord's Supper, which united the Swiss Reformed streams.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 8, “The Lord's Supper. The Consensus of Zuerich”

events.title: Peace of Augsburg
events.summary: German princes could choose between Lutheran and Catholic faith for their lands. Reformed and Anabaptist Christians were left out.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 7, “Modern Christianity. German Reformation.”

events.title: Scots Confession
events.summary: John Knox and others wrote this confession as Scotland adopted the Reformation.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Scotch Confession of Faith. A.D. 1560.”

events.title: Belgic Confession
events.summary: Written for the persecuted churches of the Low Countries, it became a standard of Dutch Reformed churches.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Belgic Confession. A.D. 1561.”

events.title: Heidelberg Catechism
events.summary: Prepared for the Palatinate, it became one of the most widely used Reformed catechisms.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Heidelberg Catechism. A.D. 1563.”

events.title: Second Helvetic Confession
events.summary: Bullinger's confession was adopted by the Swiss Reformed churches and widely received abroad.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Second Helvetic Confession. A.D. 1566.”

events.title: Thirty-Nine Articles
events.summary: The doctrinal statement of the Church of England, finalized under Elizabeth I.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “V. the Anglican Articles of Religion.”

events.title: Formula of Concord
events.summary: Settled disputes among Lutherans after Luther's death and completed the Lutheran confessions.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Form of Concord. A.D. 1577.”

events.title: The Arminian Remonstrance
events.summary: Followers of Jacob Arminius set out five articles on election, atonement, grace and perseverance.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Arminian Controversy and the Synod of Dort, A.D. 1604–1619.”
events.quote: The Arminians formularized their creed in Five Articles (drawn up by Uytenbogaert), and laid them before the representatives of Holland and West Friesland in 1610 under the name of Remonstrance, signed by forty-six ministers.

events.title: Synod of Dort
events.summary: A Reformed synod with delegates from several countries rejected the Remonstrance, and its canons are the source of the "five points of Calvinism."
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Arminian Controversy and the Synod of Dort, A.D. 1604–1619.”

events.title: Orthodox Confession of Peter Mogila
events.summary: An Eastern Orthodox statement approved in response to Catholic and Protestant teaching.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Orthodox Confession of Mogilas, A.D. 1643.”

events.title: Westminster Assembly
events.summary: The English Parliament called it to reform the Church of England. It produced the Confession and Catechisms, standards of Presbyterian churches.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Westminster Assembly.”

events.title: Peace of Westphalia
events.summary: The treaties that ended the Thirty Years' War recognized Reformed churches alongside Lutherans and Catholics in the Empire.
events.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 7, “Modern Christianity. German Reformation.”
events.quote: But it required a long and bloody struggle before Protestantism acquired equal legal rights with Romanism, and the Pope protests to this day against the Treaty of Westphalia which finally secured those rights.  § 59.

events.title: Savoy Declaration
events.summary: English Congregationalists adapted the Westminster Confession to their own church order.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “Chapter 7. The Creeds of the Evangelical Reformed Churches”

events.title: Synod of Jerusalem and Confession of Dositheus
events.summary: The Eastern church rejected Calvinist teaching attributed to Patriarch Cyril Lucaris.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Synod of Jerusalem, and the Confession of Dositheus, A.D. 1672.”

events.title: Spener's Pia Desideria and Pietism
events.summary: Spener's book set out a program of Bible study, lay participation and practical piety for German Lutherans.
events.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Pious Desires”
events.quote: outlined Pietism's basic program

events.title: The Great Awakening
events.summary: Revivals under Jonathan Edwards, George Whitefield and others spread through the American colonies and Britain.
events.source: Revival Library, “1st Great Awakening” timeline

events.title: John Wesley at Aldersgate
events.summary: Wesley's experience on 24 May 1738, hearing Luther's preface to Romans read, is often taken as a beginning of the Methodist movement.
events.source: Aldersgate SG, The Methodist Church in Singapore
events.quote: I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation.

events.title: Schleiermacher's On Religion
events.summary: Schleiermacher located religion in feeling and intuition, and is often called the father of Protestant liberalism.
events.source: Tabletalk, “The Rise of Protestant Liberalism” (2019)
events.quote: father of Protestant liberalism

events.title: Dogma of the Immaculate Conception
events.summary: Pius IX defined that Mary was preserved from original sin at her conception. Orthodox and Protestant churches don't accept this dogma.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Papal Definition of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary, A.D. 1854.”

events.title: Syllabus of Errors
events.summary: Pius IX listed modern ideas the Catholic Church then condemned, including liberalism and rationalism.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Papal Syllabus, A.D. 1864.”

events.title: First Vatican Council
events.summary: Defined papal primacy and infallibility when the pope speaks ex cathedra on faith and morals. Those who rejected the decree formed the Old Catholic churches.
events.source: Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 1, “The Vatican Decrees, Continued. The Papal Infallibility Decree.”

events.title: Azusa Street revival
events.summary: William Seymour's mission in Los Angeles became a main source of the worldwide Pentecostal movement.
events.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Azusa Street revival”

events.title: World Missionary Conference, Edinburgh
events.summary: Protestant mission leaders met at Edinburgh, in what is often seen as the formal beginning of the ecumenical movement.
events.source: Musée protestant, “The 1910 World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh”
events.quote: has been seen as the formal beginning of the Ecumenical movement

events.title: The Fundamentals
events.summary: A series of essays against theological liberalism, later seen as a foundation of Christian fundamentalism. The word "Fundamentalist" dates from 1920.
events.source: Wikipedia, “The Fundamentals”

events.title: Barth's Epistle to the Romans
events.summary: Dated 1919 and rewritten in 1921, Barth's commentary broke with liberal theology and shaped what became known as neo-orthodoxy.
events.source: Wikipedia, “Karl Barth”
events.quote: openly broke from liberal theology

events.title: Barmen Declaration
events.summary: The Confessing Church rejected the Nazi-aligned German Christians. Karl Barth was its major theological influence.
events.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Synod of Barmen”

events.title: World Council of Churches founded
events.summary: Churches founded the Council on 23 August 1948 at Amsterdam, with 147 churches taking part.
events.source: World Council of Churches, “Amsterdam 1948”

events.title: Second Vatican Council
events.summary: Opened by John XXIII and closed by Paul VI, it addressed the church, revelation, liturgy and the modern world, and opened new relations with other Christians.
events.source: EWTN, “Second Ecumenical Council of the Vatican (1962-1965)”

events.title: Catholic and Orthodox lift the 1054 excommunications
events.summary: Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras removed the mutual excommunications of 1054 from memory. Full communion was not restored.
events.source: OrthodoxWiki, “Paul VI of Rome”

events.title: Lausanne Covenant
events.summary: The International Congress on World Evangelization issued a shared evangelical statement on mission.
events.source: Lausanne Movement, “Lausanne 1974 Documents”

events.title: Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy
events.summary: More than 200 evangelical leaders, at a conference called by the International Council on Biblical Inerrancy, set out the doctrine.
events.source: Wikipedia, “Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy”

events.title: Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox agreed statement
events.summary: At Chambésy, a joint commission produced a shared statement on Christology, addressing the division over Chalcedon.
events.source: OrthodoxWiki, “Agreed Official Statements on Christology”

events.title: Common Christological Declaration
events.summary: John Paul II and Mar Dinkha IV of the Assyrian Church of the East affirmed a shared faith in Christ, addressing the division after Ephesus.
events.source: EWTN, “Common Christological Declaration”

events.title: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification
events.summary: Lutherans and Catholics signed at Augsburg a shared understanding of basic truths on justification. Methodist, Anglican and Reformed bodies later affirmed it.
events.source: Lutheran World Federation, “Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification”
